candidates.name: THE IBM SELECTRIC
candidates.epitaph: Its spinning typeball wrote the future—until the future learned to edit before printing.
candidates.why: Personal computers, word processors, and printers replaced the need for a dedicated electric typewriter.
candidates.afterlife: Restored machines, collectors, and museums preserve its distinctive mechanism and sound.
candidates.note: IBM says the Selectric was officially retired in 1986 as personal computers and printers became more popular.

rating.note: Initial editorial rating; revise after verification and preview testing.

candidates.name: GEOCITIES
candidates.epitaph: Before every profile looked alike, everyone built a strange little neighbourhood.
candidates.why: Yahoo closed the main free hosting service and directed users toward paid web hosting.
candidates.afterlife: The Internet Archive, Archive Team, and countless screenshots preserve fragments of its handmade web.
candidates.note: The main service closed on 26 October 2009; Yahoo GeoCities Japan continued until 2019.

rating.note: Initial editorial rating; revise after verification and preview testing.

candidates.name: AOL INSTANT MESSENGER
candidates.epitaph: Away messages taught a generation to be online while pretending not to be.
candidates.why: Communication shifted toward mobile messaging, social networks, and newer services built around permanent connectivity.
candidates.afterlife: Screen names, buddy lists, notification sounds, and away messages remain part of early internet memory.
candidates.note: The official announcement set the shutdown for 15 December 2017.

rating.note: Initial editorial rating; revise after verification and preview testing.

candidates.name: THE ORIGINAL ROUTEMASTER
candidates.epitaph: London kept the silhouette but retired the conductor and open platform.
candidates.why: London moved to accessible low-floor buses and one-person operation across its regular network.
candidates.afterlife: Preserved buses, private operators, and occasional heritage services keep the original design visible.
candidates.note: The end date refers to ordinary scheduled London service, not the disappearance of every Routemaster.

rating.note: Initial editorial rating; revise after verification and preview testing.

candidates.name: THE DODO
candidates.epitaph: It became the symbol of extinction after disappearing before extinction was understood.
candidates.why: Hunting, habitat disturbance, and introduced animals devastated a flightless bird adapted to life on Mauritius.
candidates.afterlife: A few remains, subfossil bones, historical descriptions, and modern reconstructions are all that survive.
candidates.note: The last reliable sighting is generally dated to 1662, although later possible dates remain debated.

rating.note: Initial editorial rating; revise after verification and preview testing.

candidates.name: PRINTED ENCYCLOPAEDIA BRITANNICA
candidates.epitaph: Thirty-two volumes became one browser tab, but the authority kept its name.
candidates.why: The publisher shifted its reference business to digital products that could be searched and continuously updated.
candidates.afterlife: Britannica continues online, while complete printed sets remain in libraries, homes, and second-hand shops.
candidates.note: The final printed edition appeared in 2010; Britannica announced the end of print publication in 2012.

rating.note: Initial editorial rating; revise after verification and preview testing.

candidates.name: THE APPLE NEWTON
candidates.epitaph: It tried to read our handwriting before computers had learned how people actually write.
candidates.why: Weak sales, a troubled launch, and Apple's renewed focus on the Macintosh ended the Newton platform.
candidates.afterlife: Its stylus, notes, apps, and handheld ambitions foreshadowed later smartphones and tablets.
candidates.note: Apple announced the end of Newton OS development and related hardware on 27 February 1998.

rating.note: Initial editorial rating; revise after verification and preview testing.

candidates.name: MINITEL
candidates.epitaph: France went online before the Web—then switched off the little terminal that took it there.
candidates.why: The open Web and modern internet services replaced France's closed videotex network and dedicated terminals.
candidates.afterlife: Preserved terminals recall an online world of directories, shopping, tickets, messages, and chat.
candidates.note: The national Minitel service launched commercially in 1982 and was shut down on 30 June 2012.

rating.note: Initial editorial rating; revise after verification and preview testing.

candidates.name: YAHOO ANSWERS
candidates.epitaph: Every question found an answer. Accuracy was optional.
candidates.why: Yahoo closed the declining question-and-answer service as users and attention moved to newer communities.
candidates.afterlife: Screenshots, memes, web archives, and quoted answers preserve its strange collective advice desk.
candidates.note: The site stopped accepting new questions in April 2021 and shut down on 4 May 2021.

rating.note: Initial editorial rating; revise after verification and preview testing.

candidates.name: THE HINDENBURG
candidates.epitaph: The age of passenger airships ended in thirty-four seconds.
candidates.why: The airship caught fire while landing at Lakehurst; the disaster destroyed public confidence in passenger zeppelins.
candidates.afterlife: Film, photographs, radio reporting, mail, and museum objects preserve the final flight and its consequences.
candidates.note: The LZ 129 entered service in 1936 and was destroyed at Lakehurst on 6 May 1937, killing 36 people.

rating.note: Initial editorial rating; revise after verification and preview testing.

candidates.name: QUEEN ELIZABETH 2
candidates.epitaph: After millions of miles, the ocean liner became a destination that no longer sailed.
candidates.why: Cunard retired and sold the ageing liner after almost forty years of transatlantic and cruise service.
candidates.afterlife: The preserved ship reopened in Dubai in 2018 as a permanently docked floating hotel.
candidates.note: QE2 entered service in 1969, retired from active service in 2008, and now survives as a hotel in Dubai.

rating.note: Initial editorial rating; revise after verification and preview testing.

candidates.name: THE QUAGGA
candidates.epitaph: Its last stripes disappeared before anyone realised there were none left.
candidates.why: Extensive hunting eliminated this distinctively patterned South African plains zebra population.
candidates.afterlife: A few skins and seven known skeletons remain, alongside photographs of one animal kept in London Zoo.
candidates.note: The last known quagga died at Amsterdam Zoo on 12 August 1883.

rating.note: Initial editorial rating; revise after verification and preview testing.

candidates.name: STELLER'S SEA COW
candidates.epitaph: Humans discovered the gentle giant—and erased it twenty-seven years later.
candidates.why: Hunters rapidly killed the slow, coastal marine mammals for their meat and fat.
candidates.afterlife: Skeletons, scattered bones, and Georg Steller's description preserve an animal never photographed alive.
candidates.note: Europeans scientifically recorded the species in 1741; it was driven to extinction by 1768.

rating.note: Initial editorial rating; revise after verification and preview testing.

candidates.name: THE PAPER AIRLINE TICKET
candidates.epitaph: The journey once began with a document too valuable to lose.
candidates.why: Electronic ticket records were cheaper, easier to update, and impossible for passengers to leave at home.
candidates.afterlife: Old ticket wallets, coupons, stubs, and collectors preserve the paperwork of commercial flight.
candidates.note: The date refers specifically to IATA ending paper ticket stock for its agency system on 1 June 2008, not every paper travel document.

rating.note: Initial editorial rating; revise after verification and preview testing.

candidates.name: WINDOWS PHONE
candidates.epitaph: Its tiles were different, elegant—and surrounded by apps that never arrived.
candidates.why: Limited market share and a persistent shortage of major apps left Microsoft's mobile platform behind Android and iOS.
candidates.afterlife: Lumia hardware, Metro design, live tiles, and surviving devices preserve Microsoft's distinct phone interface.
candidates.note: The 2019 date marks Microsoft's stated end of support for the final Windows 10 Mobile release; some services and one additional update continued briefly.

rating.note: Initial editorial rating; revise after verification and preview testing.

candidates.name: ICQ
candidates.epitaph: Before profiles and feeds, a number and an “Uh-oh!” meant someone was there.
candidates.why: Mobile-first messaging platforms and social networks gradually replaced the pioneering desktop messenger.
candidates.afterlife: Its numeric user IDs, flower symbol, notification sound, and influence survive in the history of online chat.
candidates.note: ICQ's operator announced that the service would stop on 26 June 2024; preserve a secondary source because the official shutdown page may change.

rating.note: Initial editorial rating; revise after verification and preview testing.

candidates.name: RMS QUEEN MARY PASSENGER SERVICE
candidates.epitaph: The Atlantic crossing became a destination only after the aeroplane made it unnecessary.
candidates.why: Jet airliners made scheduled transatlantic sea travel slower and less competitive, and Cunard retired the ageing liner.
candidates.afterlife: Queen Mary remains permanently moored in Long Beach as a preserved ship, hotel, museum, and event venue.
candidates.note: Only the ship's active passenger service is gone. The vessel survives and remains open to visitors.

rating.note: Initial editorial rating; revise after verification and preview testing.

candidates.name: THE CAROLINA PARAKEET
candidates.epitaph: North America once had a native parrot. Its forests became quiet within a human lifetime.
candidates.why: Habitat loss, killing as an agricultural pest, feather hunting, and possibly disease drove the species into rapid decline.
candidates.afterlife: Museum skins, eggs, skeletal material, historical paintings, and written accounts preserve its vivid appearance.
candidates.note: The last known bird, Incas, died at Cincinnati Zoo on 21 February 1918; the causes of the species' extinction remain partly uncertain.

rating.note: Initial editorial rating; revise after verification and preview testing.

candidates.name: THE PYRENEAN IBEX
candidates.epitaph: The last one died beneath a fallen tree—and briefly returned as a clone three years later.
candidates.why: Hunting and other pressures reduced it to one individual, although the precise causes of decline remain disputed.
candidates.afterlife: Preserved tissue produced a clone in 2003; she lived only minutes—the first extinct taxon briefly cloned alive.
candidates.note: The last natural individual died in January 2000. The cloning claim and taxonomic wording require specialist-source verification before promotion.

rating.note: Initial editorial rating; revise after verification and preview testing.

candidates.name: INTERNET EXPLORER
candidates.epitaph: For years, the web arrived through a blue ‘e’—whether users chose it or not.
candidates.why: Modern browsers overtook it while Microsoft replaced it with Edge and retired the IE11 desktop application.
candidates.afterlife: IE mode and Trident compatibility remain available for organisations that still depend on legacy websites.
candidates.note: The 2022 date applies to the Internet Explorer 11 desktop application on certain Windows 10 versions; IE mode remains supported in Microsoft Edge.

rating.note: Initial editorial rating; revise after verification and preview testing.

candidates.name: CERN'S LEP COLLIDER
candidates.epitaph: Its particles stopped circling so a bigger question could use the same tunnel.
candidates.why: CERN dismantled the electron-positron collider to install the Large Hadron Collider in its 27-kilometre tunnel.
candidates.afterlife: Its precision measurements remain, and the LHC reuses the tunnel beneath the French-Swiss border.
candidates.note: First beam: 14 July 1989. LEP closed on 2 November 2000; the reused tunnel is not itself gone.

rating.note: Strong science story and clear retirement; a tunnel scene needs careful identification.

candidates.name: ST HELENA GIANT EARWIG
candidates.epitaph: Even the world's largest earwig could disappear beneath our notice.
candidates.why: Habitat loss and introduced species likely contributed to its disappearance from its only island home.
candidates.afterlife: Museum specimens preserve its extraordinary size and the story of St Helena's lost wildlife.
candidates.note: 1967 is the last reported live record, not a proven extinction date. IUCN listed it Extinct in 2014; verify the current assessment before promotion.

rating.note: Distinctive insect broadens Nature; exact extinction date and causes require qualified wording.

candidates.name: CASSINI
candidates.epitaph: It became part of the world it had spent thirteen years revealing.
candidates.why: With fuel running low, Cassini was sent into Saturn to protect potentially habitable moons from contamination.
candidates.afterlife: Its images and scientific data keep revealing Saturn, its rings, and its moons long after the final signal.
candidates.note: Dates run from launch in 1997 to intentional atmospheric entry on 15 September 2017. This entry is the orbiter, not the Huygens lander.

rating.note: Strong deliberate farewell, precise endpoint and distinctive spacecraft; verify instrument geometry before artwork.

candidates.name: THE HUIA
candidates.epitaph: Its white-tipped feathers outlasted the forest voice that wore them.
candidates.why: Introduced mammal predators and hunting likely drove this New Zealand forest bird to extinction.
candidates.afterlife: Museum specimens and its enduring cultural significance preserve the memory of this distinctive bird.
candidates.note: 1907 is the last accepted sighting. Some huia likely survived into the 1920s; the exact extinction date is unknown.

rating.note: Distinctive bill dimorphism and cultural story; uncertain final date must remain qualified.

candidates.name: BBC CEEFAX
candidates.epitaph: Before the web, news arrived one numbered page at a time.
candidates.why: The UK’s digital television switchover ended the analogue signal that carried the original teletext service.
candidates.afterlife: Archives, recreations, and its blocky visual language preserve a pre-web way of browsing information.
candidates.note: Ceefax launched in 1974 and ended with the final UK analogue television switchover on 23 October 2012.

rating.note: A clear analogue endpoint and instantly distinctive screen language; recognition is strongest in the UK.

candidates.name: THE ORIGINAL PENN STATION
candidates.epitaph: New York tore down a gateway grand enough to make arrival feel like an event.
candidates.why: Declining rail traffic and a redevelopment deal traded its above-ground halls for Madison Square Garden.
candidates.afterlife: Surviving fragments, photographs, and the preservation movement born from its loss keep the station present.
candidates.source_name: Museum of the City of New York
candidates.note: 1963 marks the start of demolition; the above-ground building was removed by 1966 while the underground station continued.

rating.note: A visually powerful loss with a major preservation afterlife; the asterisk distinguishes demolition’s start from completion.

rating_system.purpose: Prioritisation only. Ratings do not replace the verification gate.
rating_system.scale: Each dimension is scored from 1 (weak) to 5 (excellent); total is out of 25.

dimensions.recognition: How readily a broad audience recognises or connects with the subject.
dimensions.visual_strength: How distinctive and readable the subject can be in monochrome e-ink artwork.
dimensions.story_strength: How well the disappearance supports a concise, memorable museum card.
dimensions.endpoint_clarity: How clearly the ending date and status can be defined without misleading claims.
dimensions.catalogue_fit: How well the entry adds variety and matches GOODBYE's curatorial voice.
